props.title: I Am Not Your Negro

sections.content: **I Am Not Your Negro** (2016) revolutionized the documentary format by transforming James Baldwin's unfinished manuscript into a searing examination of American racism. Director Raoul Peck masterfully weaves Baldwin's words (narrated by Samuel L. Jackson) with archival footage and contemporary images, creating haunting parallels between Civil Rights-era violence and modern racial injustice. The film follows Baldwin's personal reflections on three murdered friends - Medgar Evers, Malcolm X, and Martin Luther King Jr. - while expanding into a broader critique of white America's self-deception about racism. Like Spike Lee's Do The Right Thing (1989) and Ava DuVernay's 13th (2016), it forces viewers to confront uncomfortable truths about systemic racism.

sections.content: Baldwin's prophetic observations gain new urgency through Peck's brilliant juxtaposition of past and present imagery. The film's technique recalls other groundbreaking documentary works like **The Act of Killing** (2012) and **Stories We Tell** (2012), which similarly blur the lines between past and present, personal and political. Peck's decision to incorporate modern footage of Ferguson, Black Lives Matter protests, and police violence demonstrates Baldwin's continued relevance while suggesting America's fundamental relationship with race remains unchanged. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Black Documentary Cinema

**I Am Not Your Negro** joins a vital tradition of documentaries examining Black American experience, from William Greaves' **Symbiopsychotaxiplasm: Take One** (1968) to Stanley Nelson's The Black Panthers: Vanguard of the Revolution (2015). What distinguishes Peck's film is its refusal to simply document history - instead, it creates an urgent dialogue between past and present. The film's innovative structure influenced later works like Time (2020) and MLK/FBI (2020), which similarly use archival footage to expose historical continuities of racial oppression.
